## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  EA Collaborative Learning — SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet: "Programme d'approfondissement — EA Collaborative Learning" (occurrence: "EA - Collaborative Learning", X3A MA3, applied mathematics department); the 2025-2026 sheet of the same course unit was titled "Emerging Topics in Machine Learning - Collaborative Learning", hence the name of these materials
  Code                    APM_51178_EP
  Team and workload       Course coordinators: El Mahdi El Mhamdi & Paul Mangold (occurrence coordinator: Paul Mangold, École Polytechnique, CMAP) · 36 h in person (lecture/tutorial/lab split not published on the sheet, enrollment / 42) · 4.5 ECTS (value retained for the LLGA; 5 ECTS for the École Polytechnique degree, the MJH masters and exchange programs) · teaching languages: French and English · distributed and federated learning, Byzantine robustness, differential privacy, and scaling models — the "systems" viewpoint on LLMs.
  Status in the program   [Recommended — LLGA track]{.badge .recommended} M1 · S1 / period 1 (fall semester, from 17/09/26 to 18/12/26)
  ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who deploys ML and hits distribution, federated learning, robustness. **Empirical first**: FedAvg that stalls as soon as 3 clients are Byzantine; DP-SGD that costs −6 accuracy points for ε=8; then we name robust aggregation, DP composition, scaling.

Distributed / federated learning, Byzantine robustness, privacy — the systems view of LLMs (CMAP).

### What you will be able to do

-   Analyze distributed stochastic gradient descent: convergence speed, the effect of mini-batch size, step size, and number of workers.
-   Distinguish distributed learning architectures (centralized, local, federated) and their communication/computation trade-offs.
-   Explain the federated learning model (FedAvg) and its assumptions, in particular data heterogeneity across clients.
-   Identify Byzantine failures in a learning cluster and apply the robust aggregation rules that neutralize them.
-   Define differential privacy (ε-differential privacy), apply it to SGD, and interpret the utility/privacy trade-off.
-   Reason about collaboration challenges: per-client personalization, fairness across participants, incentives.
-   Estimate the cost of a training run (scaling models and compute) and read the scaling laws that structure the field.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

### Where this course fits in the program

Recommended option of the LLGA track in Year 1 · Period 1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS). The official sheet recommends MAP433 for students of the engineering cycle; in practice, this module assumes the optimization foundation of the [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) module, whose opening chapter covers the analysis of SGD — extended here to the distributed case — and the theory of generalization. The two refreshers ([Refresher in Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html), [Refresher in Computer Science](../m1p1-refresher-cs/index.html)) are its upstream prerequisites. The course unit is shared with the engineering cycle (X), the MJH master, exchange programs and the MScT IoT and TRAI tracks.

Downstream, this module opens three directions. [Privacy and Uncertainty Quantification](../m2-privacy-uncertainty/index.html) (M2) extends the differential privacy seen here toward private inference and uncertainty quantification; [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) (M2) picks up scaling and the systems viewpoint for industrializing LLMs; [Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) (Period 2) draws on the same questions of collaboration and multiple agents, up to multi-agent RL.

### Course outline

-   **Review: SGD and its analysis**: convergence of stochastic gradient descent, taken from the Machine Learning module and extended to distributed systems.
-   **Landscape of emerging topics**: a map of the research fronts that structure large-scale ML today.
-   **Distributed learning**: parallelizing training, synchronizing workers, arbitrating between communication and computation.
-   **Federated learning**: learning on data that never leaves its owners — the FedAvg framework and its variants.
-   **Byzantine robustness**: detecting and tolerating faulty or malicious workers in aggregation.
-   **Differential privacy**: formalizing and guaranteeing the protection of individuals during training.
-   **Collaboration, personalization, fairness**: learning models together that remain useful to everyone — and fair.
-   **Scaling and compute**: what large models cost, and what the field's scaling laws say.
-   **Course research notes — CMAP (El Mhamdi, Dieuleveut)**: the research of El Mahdi El Mhamdi (Byzantine robustness) and Aymeric Dieuleveut (stochastic SGD, federated learning), CMAP — the official 2026-2027 team being El Mhamdi & Mangold.

### How to study this module

-   First secure your understanding of SGD analysis: the review chapter is short, but mastering it is a prerequisite for all the distributed and federated chapters.
-   For each aggregation scheme (mean, median, trimmed mean), ask yourself "what happens with a malicious worker?" — that is the course's guiding thread.
-   Simulate a small federated learning setup with clients holding heterogeneous data: the gap between homogeneous theory and heterogeneous practice can only be understood by running it.
-   Do the differential privacy exercises on paper: composing mechanisms, computing an ε budget, interpreting a guarantee.
-   Follow the news on scaling laws and compute in parallel with the scaling chapter: that chapter ages the fastest, and critical reading is the targeted skill.
-   If you need a refresher on the basics, go back to the [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) module: optimization and concentration are covered there at the level expected here.

::: note
[Note Extrapolons]{.tag} The LLGA master's program trains students to work with large models deployed in real organizations: sensitive data, distributed teams, compute budgets. This module teaches exactly what separates a notebook prototype from a trustworthy AI system — the shared culture of the LLGA engineer and of the researcher who will formalize these guarantees.
:::

## 0. Review: SGD and its analysis {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3/M1 review — the stochastic foundation
:::

-   **Gradient descent**: $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla f(\theta_t)$; convex and $L$-smooth ⇒ $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ decrease.
-   **SGD**: replace $\nabla f$ with a batch gradient $g_t = \frac1m \sum_{i \in B_t} \nabla \ell(\theta_t; x_i)$, unbiased, $\mathrm{Var}(g_t) = \mathcal{O}(1/m)$ (CLT, see the Refresher Statistics module).
-   **Strong convexity**: $f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \leq \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda) f(y) - \tfrac{\mu}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\\|x - y\\|^2$ ⇒ linear convergence in the deterministic case, $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ in the stochastic case.
-   **Descent inequality**: for $f$ $L$-smooth, $f(\theta_{t+1}) \leq f(\theta_t) - \eta(1 - \tfrac{\eta L}{2})\\|\nabla f(\theta_t)\\|^2$ — the basic lemma for this entire chapter.
::::

::: def
[Working assumptions (A1)-(A3)]{.tag} (A1) $f$ convex, $L$-smooth, with minimizer $\theta^\star$ (write $D = \\|\theta_0 - \theta^\star\\|$, $f^\star = f(\theta^\star)$); (A2) unbiased stochastic gradient $\mathbb{E}[g_t \mid \theta_t] = \nabla f(\theta_t)$; (A3) bounded variance $\mathbb{E}\\|g_t - \nabla f(\theta_t)\\|^2 \leq \sigma^2$. We write $g_t = \nabla f(\theta_t) + \xi_t$ with $\mathbb{E}\xi_t = 0$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Constant-step SGD: full proof]{.tag} Under (A1)-(A3), with step size $\eta \leq \frac{1}{2L}$: $$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \mathbb{E}\big[f(\theta_t) - f^\star\big] \;\leq\; \frac{D^2}{2\eta T} \;+\; \frac{\eta \sigma^2}{2} \;\leq\; \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{L D^2}{T}\Big) + \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt T}\Big),$$ the last term being obtained for $\eta = \min\big(\tfrac{1}{2L}, \tfrac{D}{\sigma\sqrt T}\big)$.

::: proof
**Step 1 (recursion on the distances).** With $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta g_t$ and $\mathbb{E}[\xi_t \mid \theta_t] = 0$ (the cross term vanishes): $$\mathbb{E}\\|\theta_{t+1} - \theta^\star\\|^2 = \\|\theta_t - \theta^\star\\|^2 - 2\eta \big\langle \nabla f(\theta_t),\, \theta_t - \theta^\star \big\rangle + \eta^2\, \mathbb{E}\\|g_t\\|^2.$$ **Step 2 (the three ingredients).** (i) convexity: $\langle \nabla f(\theta_t), \theta_t - \theta^\star\rangle \geq f(\theta_t) - f^\star$; (ii) bias-variance decomposition + smoothness: $\mathbb{E}\\|g_t\\|^2 = \\|\nabla f(\theta_t)\\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\\|\xi_t\\|^2 \leq 2L\big(f(\theta_t) - f^\star\big) + \sigma^2$ (since $\\|\nabla f(\theta)\\|^2 \leq 2L(f(\theta) - f^\star)$ for $f$ convex and $L$-smooth); combining: $$\mathbb{E}\\|\theta_{t+1} - \theta^\star\\|^2 \;\leq\; \mathbb{E}\\|\theta_t - \theta^\star\\|^2 \;-\; 2\eta(1 - \eta L)\,\mathbb{E}[f(\theta_t) - f^\star] \;+\; \eta^2 \sigma^2.$$ **Step 3 (telescoping).** Sum over $t = 0, \dots, T-1$: the sum of the distances telescopes to $D^2$, so with $\eta \leq \frac{1}{2L}$ (hence $1 - \eta L \geq \tfrac12$): $$\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \mathbb{E}[f(\theta_t) - f^\star] \;\leq\; \frac{D^2}{2\eta T} + \frac{\eta \sigma^2}{2}. \qquad \blacksquare$$
:::

*Reading.* Two terms: optimization ($D^2/\eta T$, vanishes with $T$) and statistics ($\eta\sigma^2$, the "floor" of the constant step size); the choice of $\eta$ arbitrates. In practice, networks are trained with constant step sizes (or step sizes decreasing in stages); with a decreasing step size $\eta_t \propto 1/t$, the average of the iterates reaches $\mathcal{O}(\log T / T)$, and $\mathcal{O}(\sigma^2 / \mu T)$ if $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex.
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Lower bounds (statements)]{.tag} (i) *Stochastic oracle* (Nemirovski-Yudin): for any algorithm accessing $f$ only through noisy gradients of variance $\sigma^2$, there exists a convex, $L$-smooth function such that $\mathbb{E}[f(\hat\theta_T) - f^\star] \geq c\, \sigma D/\sqrt T$ — the rate of Theorem 0.1 is therefore *optimal*; the noise is not a flaw of the algorithm but a law of the problem. (ii) *Strongly convex*: the bound becomes $\Omega(\sigma^2/\mu T)$: the statistical floor cannot be beaten, even with all the available structure. *Consequence for this module*: parallelizing (ch. 2) can do no better than reducing $\sigma$ — which is exactly what the aggregation of $K$ workers does.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Variance reduction: SAGA and SVRG (sketch)]{.tag} The $\sigma/\sqrt T$ floor comes from the *constant* variance of the gradient; on a finite sum $f = \frac1n \sum_i f_i$, it can be made to decrease:

-   **SVRG** (Johnson & Zhang): periodically compute the exact gradient $\nabla f(\tilde\theta)$ at a reference point $\tilde\theta$, then use the *control variate* $v_t = \nabla f_{i_t}(\theta_t) - \nabla f_{i_t}(\tilde\theta) + \nabla f(\tilde\theta)$: unbiased, and with variance proportional to $\\|\theta_t - \tilde\theta\\|^2$ — which decreases over the course of the optimization; linear rate $\mathcal{O}((n + \kappa)\log 1/\varepsilon)$ (versus $\mathcal{O}(n\kappa \log 1/\varepsilon)$ for GD);
-   **SAGA**: keep in a table the latest $\nabla f_i$ seen for each $i$ and correct by their average — same effect, without periodic recomputation.

These *control variate* ideas will reappear in federated learning (SCAFFOLD, ch. 3) and in the Byzantine setting (Bulyan, ch. 8): this is THE algorithmic motif of the module.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Momentum, Nesterov, sampling]{.tag} **Momentum** (heavy ball): $v_{t+1} = \beta v_t + g_t$, $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta v_{t+1}$ — damps oscillations along steep directions (poorly conditioned gradient covariance matrix); typical choice $\beta = 0.9$. **Nesterov**: evaluate the gradient at the anticipated point $\theta_t - \gamma v_t$; in the deterministic case, the rate goes from $\mathcal{O}(LD^2/T)$ to $\mathcal{O}(LD^2/T^2)$ — optimal for a first-order method. **Weighted sampling**: draw $i$ according to a distribution $q$ and correct with $g = \nabla f_i/q(i)$; the variance is minimized when $q_i \propto \\|\nabla f_i\\|$ (importance sampling, Zhao & Zhang, 2014); the *stratified* variant partitions the data into homogeneous strata and allocates the sampling budget where the internal variance is large — stratification reduces $\sigma^2$ even before parallelizing.
:::

## 1. Landscape of emerging topics {#ch1}

Concrete scene: 50 hospital clients, 2 malicious. Gradient averaging pulls the model toward a backdoor. This chapter sets the threat model before recipes.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Trusting the mean (Byzantine); releasing a model with no DP budget; scaling the batch without retuning noise / learning rate.
:::

This module opens with the questions that structure current research and industry, in direct preparation for the M2 modules (LLMs, Explainability/Security/Privacy):

-   **Scaling laws**: power-law loss as a function of data/parameters/compute (Kaplan 2020, Hoffmann/Chinchilla 2022 — chapter 7); emergence of capabilities; compute as a scarce resource;
-   **Distributed training** of large models: data/tensor/pipeline parallelism, MoE (chapters 2 and 7);
-   **Frugal fine-tuning**: LoRA and adapters — the "collaboration" between a large central model and local uses (chapters 3 and 7);
-   **Trustworthy?** Robustness to malicious clients, privacy of training data, fairness across participants — the three guiding threads of chapters 4-6;
-   **Collaborative agents**: multi-agent orchestration = collaboration of models (direct link with the Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents module, chapter 7, and with "graph engineering").

## 2. Distributed learning {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Distributed SGD (synchronous workers)]{.tag} $K$ workers hold data shards. At each step: each worker $k$ computes $g^{(k)}$ on its mini-batch, the server aggregates and broadcasts: $$\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \frac1K \sum_{k=1}^K g_t^{(k)}.$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Linear speedup (proof via the variance)]{.tag} If the $g_t^{(k)}$ are independent, unbiased, with variance $\sigma^2$, then $\bar g_t = \frac1K \sum_k g_t^{(k)}$ is unbiased with $$\mathbb{E}\\|\bar g_t\\|^2 = \\|\nabla f\\|^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{K},$$ and Theorem 0.1 applies with $\sigma \to \sigma/\sqrt K$: $$\frac1T \sum_t \mathbb{E}[f(\theta_t) - f^\star] \leq \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{LD^2}{T} + \frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt{KT}}\Big).$$

::: proof
Independence + unbiasedness: $\mathbb{E}\\|\bar g\\|^2 = \\|\mathbb{E}\bar g\\|^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\bar g) = \\|\nabla f\\|^2 + \frac{1}{K^2}\sum_k \mathrm{Var}(g^{(k)}) = \\|\nabla f\\|^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{K}$. To reach a target accuracy $\varepsilon = \sigma D/\sqrt{T}$, one needs $T(\varepsilon) \propto \frac{\sigma^2 D^2}{K\,\varepsilon^2}$ distributed iterations — versus $\frac{\sigma^2 D^2}{\varepsilon^2}$ sequentially: **$K$ times fewer iterations**, each $K$ times more expensive in computation (parallelized): this is the *ideal* linear speedup, valid if and only if communication is negligible — which it never is (rest of this chapter). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The communication wall]{.tag} Sending a gradient of $10^9$ parameters (4 GB in fp32) costs more than computing it. Ring all-reduce is bandwidth-optimal: each worker only exchanges $\frac{2(K-1)}{K}$ model sizes per step. The rest of this chapter aims to *reduce the bytes exchanged*.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Quantization: QSGD (Alistarh et al., 2017)]{.tag} Quantize each coordinate $v_i$ by random rounding to the grid $\{0, \pm s^{-1}\\|v\\|_2, \dots, \pm\\|v\\|_2\}$: the quantizer $Q_s$ is *unbiased* and $$\mathbb{E}\\|Q_s(v)\\|^2 \;\leq\; \Big(1 + \min\Big\{\frac{d}{s^2}, \frac{\sqrt d}{s}\Big\}\Big) \\|v\\|^2.$$ Reading: with $s = \sqrt d$ levels, the variance barely doubles, and the (entropy) coding of the quantized tensor costs only $\sim d/2$ bits per coordinate instead of 32 — up to an order of magnitude of bandwidth saved at equal training quality. Extreme case: **signSGD** (1 bit per coordinate: the sign); combined with *majority vote* it converges under adapted assumptions (Bernstein et al., 2019). The general trade-off: bits ↔ variance (Theorem 2.2: more variance = less speedup).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Sparsification and error feedback]{.tag} Sending only the $k$ largest coordinates (top-k) drastically reduces communication — but the truncated gradient is *biased*, and top-k alone can make training diverge. **Error feedback**: keep the residual: $$e_{t+1} = \big(g_t + e_t\big) - \mathrm{Top}_k\big(g_t + e_t\big), \qquad \text{one sends } \mathrm{Top}_k(g_t + e_t),$$ each "forgotten" coordinate is eventually sent once its accumulated residual enters the top-k: convergence is restored at the rate of uncompressed SGD (Seide et al. 2014 for 1-bit; analyses by Stich et al. 2018). In practice: top-k at 1% + error feedback is nearly free in quality.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Asynchrony and Hogwild!]{.tag} Synchronizing $K$ workers means waiting for the slowest one (the "stragglers"). In *asynchronous* mode, each worker pushes its gradient computed on a model potentially stale by $\tau$ steps (*staleness*): the bound of Theorem 0.1 degrades by a factor $(1 + \tau)$. **Hogwild!** (Recht et al., 2011): lock-free SGD on shared memory, valid for *sparse* problems (concurrent updates rarely collide); Lian et al. (2015): asynchronous SGD retains the $1/\sqrt T$ and the linear speedup up to constant staleness — asynchrony pays off when clock variance dominates.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Decentralized: gossip and the graph spectrum]{.tag} Without a server: the workers form a communication graph $\mathcal{G}$ (adjacency matrix $A$, Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$) and exchange with their neighbors. *Gossip aggregation* (matrix $W$ doubly stochastic, e.g. $W = I - \gamma \mathcal{L}$): $$\theta^{(k)} \leftarrow \sum_j W_{kj}\, \theta^{(j)}$$ makes all nodes converge to the average at geometric speed $$\big\\|\theta_t - \bar\theta \,\mathbf{1}\big\\| \;\leq\; \rho(W)^t\, \\|\theta_0 - \bar\theta\,\mathbf{1}\\|, \qquad \rho(W) = \max_{i \neq 1} \|\lambda_i(W)\| = 1 - \lambda_2,$$ where $\lambda_2$ is the *spectral gap* (algebraic connectivity of the graph — see the Graph ML module, spectrum chapter; chain = slow, complete graph = fast, expander = nearly optimal). **Decentralized SGD** (D-PSGD, Lian et al., ICML 2017) interleaves local SGD steps and gossip: it retains the $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt T)$ rate of the centralized version *and* its linear speedup, with local exchanges instead of the global all-reduce — it *would beat* the centralized version in wall-clock time as soon as the graph is well connected and bandwidth is limited.
:::

  Architecture               Communication/step   Fault tolerance            Hard point
  -------------------------- -------------------- -------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Synchronous centralized    global all-reduce    low (a straggler blocks)   collective latency
  Asynchronous centralized   individual push      good                       staleness, consistency
  Decentralized (gossip)     neighborhood only    excellent                  factor $1/\lambda_2$ in the rate

::: note
[LLM connection]{.tag} A typical LLM training run mobilizes thousands of GPUs: the choices of data-parallel vs pipeline vs tensor (splitting the model itself, ZeRO: sharding of optimizer states) are choices of algebra and communication — lab topics in this module, explored further in M2 (ML Ops). The methods of this chapter (quantization, error feedback) apply as-is to LLM gradients.
:::

## 3. Federated learning {#ch3}

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.1 — FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017)]{.tag} Clients $\{1..K\}$ with local data $\mathcal{D}_k$ that is *non-iid* (each has its own data, never shared). At each round:

1.  the server broadcasts $\theta_r$ to a subset of clients;
2.  each client $k$ performs $E$ epochs of local SGD: $\theta_r^{(k)} \approx \arg\min F_k$;
3.  weighted aggregation: $\theta_{r+1} = \sum_k \tfrac{n_k}{n}\, \theta_r^{(k)}$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Client drift: proving it on a quadratic example]{.tag} Heterogeneity makes clients drift: local SGD solves *their* own problems before aggregation. Exact computation on $F_k(\theta) = \tfrac{a_k}{2}(\theta - z_k)^2$ (local SGD = exact gradient, step size $\eta$):

::: proof
One local step: $\theta \leftarrow (1 - \eta a_k)\theta + \eta a_k z_k$, so after $E$ steps starting from $\theta_r$ (geometric sum): $$\theta_r^{(k)} = z_k + c_k\,(\theta_r - z_k), \qquad c_k = (1 - \eta a_k)^E.$$ The aggregation $\theta_{r+1} = \frac1K\sum_k \theta_r^{(k)}$ is an affine iteration whose fixed point satisfies $\theta_\infty = \frac1K\sum_k (1 - c_k)\, z_k \,\Big/\, \frac1K \sum_k (1 - c_k)$ — a *weighted average by the effective curvatures* $1 - c_k$. Now the global optimum of $F = \frac1K\sum F_k$ is $\theta^\star = \sum a_k z_k / \sum a_k$. The two coincide only if the $a_k$ are equal: **FedAvg converges to a point that is NOT the global optimum** as soon as the curvatures differ. *Numbers.* $K=2$, $a_1 = 1, z_1 = 0$, $a_2 = 10, z_2 = 1$, $\eta = 0.05$, $E = 10$: $c_1 = 0.95^{10} \approx 0.60$, $c_2 = 0.5^{10} \approx 0.001$; $\theta^\star = 10/11 \approx 0.909$, but $\theta_\infty = \frac{1 \cdot 1}{0.40 + 1} \approx 0.713$: a structural bias of \~20% that does *not* vanish as the number of rounds grows. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Convergence of FedAvg (convex setting, statement)]{.tag} Under (A1)-(A3) per client and bounded heterogeneity, the Theorem-0.1-style analysis applied to FedAvg (Li et al., 2020) yields, with $E$ local steps per round of $K$ clients: $$\mathbb{E}\big[F(\theta_R)\big] - F^\star \;\leq\; \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{D^2}{\eta E R}\Big) + \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2 K E R}\Big) + \mathcal{O}\big(\Gamma\big), \qquad \Gamma = F^\star - \sum_k \frac{n_k}{n} F_k^\star \ \text{(or equivalent)},$$ where the **heterogeneity term** $\Gamma \> 0$ measures the gap between the global optimum and the local optima: it is the analytic manifestation of Theorem 3.2. The first two terms decrease with the rounds (communication gain: $E$ steps for 1 exchange); the third is a bias that only a *correction* (SCAFFOLD) or a *penalty* (FedProx) can mitigate.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — FedProx: the role of the proximal term]{.tag} FedProx (Li et al., 2020): each client minimizes a *regularized* objective $$\theta^{(k)} \approx \arg\min_\theta\ F_k(\theta) + \frac{\mu}{2}\\|\theta - \theta_r\\|^2,$$ then aggregates. The proximal penalty (i) curbs the drift of Theorem 3.2 — the client stays in a neighborhood of $\theta_r$ of radius $\propto 1/\mu$; (ii) makes $E$ arbitrary (tolerance to slow or partial clients — work with what has been received); (iii) can be read as a proximal step of the global problem: in the limit $\mu \to \infty$, FedAvg with 1 step. Trade-off: too large a $\mu$ crushes local work (back to communication-slow FedSGD), too small a $\mu$ lets clients drift.
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.5 — SCAFFOLD: variance correction via control variates]{.tag} (Karimireddy et al., ICML 2020.) The server and the clients maintain *control variates* $c$ and $c_k$ (initially zero). Local step: $$\theta_{j+1}^{(k)} = \theta_j^{(k)} - \eta\big(g_k(\theta_j^{(k)}) - c_k + c\big),$$ update of the client control at the end of the round: $$c_k^{+} = c_k - c + \frac{\theta_r - \theta_E^{(k)}}{\eta E}, \qquad c^{+} = \frac1K \sum_k c_k^{+}.$$ *Reading.* The term $-c_k + c$ replaces the local gradient with a "recentered" version: $c_k - c$ estimates the mean difference between the local gradient and the global gradient — exactly the drift of Theorem 3.2. On the quadratic example above, the correction is *exact*: the drift disappears and the fixed point becomes $\theta^\star$ again (exercise 4). Result: the number of rounds to reach $\varepsilon$ goes from $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)$ (FedAvg, with large $E$) to $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ — the same motif as SVRG (Proposition 0.3): a control variate buys a factor of $\varepsilon$.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Personalization: Ditto and local fine-tuning]{.tag} When clients *want* different models (hospitals with distinct practices), heterogeneity becomes a resource: learn a good global model that serves as an initialization for everyone, then personalize. **Ditto** (Li et al., 2021) solves, per client, $$\min_{\theta_k}\ F_k(\theta_k) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\\|\theta_k - \theta^\star_{\mathrm{glob}}\\|^2$$ jointly with the global problem: $\lambda$ arbitrates specialization/collaboration — and the solution improves *fairness* across clients (the worst client is not sacrificed for the benefit of the average client). Pragmatic version: local fine-tuning of the federated model (standard in production, e.g. keyboards); probabilistic version: mixtures of posteriors (see ch. 8, FedEM).
:::

                    Cross-silo                       Cross-device
  ----------------- -------------------------------- --------------------------------------
  Clients           2 – 100 (hospitals, banks)       10⁶ – 10⁹ (phones)
  Availability      nearly permanent                 episodic, battery/network
  Local state       possible (controls, histories)   minimal (SCAFFOLD costly)
  Main constraint   data heterogeneity               communication, partial participation

::: note
[Applications and LLMs]{.tag} Healthcare (hospital consortia, data that cannot be centralized), mobile keyboards (next-word prediction, Gboard), finance. For LLMs: federating *LoRA adapters* (the model is frozen, only the small rank-$r$ matrices $A, B$ are exchanged) — demonstrated for instruction tuning (FedIT, Zhang et al., 2023); open questions: heterogeneity of local instructions, noise from small batches, privacy of prompts (chapter 5), robustness to hostile clients (chapter 4). M2 project topic.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def fedavg(clients, rounds=50, E=5, eta=0.1):
    """clients: list of local functions (theta -> theta after E SGD steps)."""
    theta = np.zeros(d)
    for r in range(rounds):
        local = [c(theta, E, eta) for c in clients]   # local phase
        theta = np.mean(local, axis=0)                # aggregation
    return theta

# SCAFFOLD: add the control variates
def scaffold(clients, rounds=50, E=5, eta=0.1):
    theta = np.zeros(d); c = np.zeros(d)
    ck = [np.zeros(d) for _ in clients]
    for r in range(rounds):
        new_ck, loc = [], []
        for k, client in enumerate(clients):
            theta_k, drift = client(theta, E, eta, correction=c - ck[k])
            loc.append(theta_k)
            new_ck.append(ck[k] - c + (theta - theta_k) / (eta * E))
        theta = np.mean(loc, axis=0)
        ck, c = new_ck, np.mean(ck, axis=0)
    return theta
```

## 4. Byzantine robustness {#ch4}

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Byzantine client and threat model]{.tag} A client is **Byzantine** if it returns an arbitrary gradient (crash *or* attack: data poisoning, model poisoning, backdoor). One distinguishes:

  Failure                       Behavior                                       Tolerance threshold
  ----------------------------- ---------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------
  Crash                         stops responding                               redundancy, timeout (systems)
  Byzantine (statistical)       arbitrary message, honest iid gradients        $f \< K/2$ (geometric rules)
  Byzantine (exact agreement)   arbitrary message, no statistical assumption   $f \< K/3$ (information-theoretic bounds)

The battle is fought on the **aggregation rule** (GAR): replace the mean with a robust operator — the rest of the pipeline (ch. 2-3) is unchanged.
:::

::: ex
[Attacks, by hand]{.tag}

-   **Label flipping**: the client trains on flipped labels — its gradient points opposite to the consensus;
-   **Large-scale model poisoning**: in dimension 1, honest $\mu = 0.5$, $K = 10$, $f = 1$ attacker sending $C = \tfrac{K-f}{f}\mu + 1 = 5.5$: $\mathrm{mean} = \frac{9 \times 0.5 - 5.5}{10} = -0.1$ — the sign is *reversed* by a single client: the mean is uncontrolled as soon as $f \geq 1$ (norm of the bias arbitrarily large);
-   **Backdoor**: data with a trigger ("add word X to every sentence containing the secret sequence"); the poisoned model keeps normal accuracy on clean data and fires on the trigger — invisible in the global metric, dangerous in deployment.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Median and trimmed mean: guarantees in dimension 1 (proved)]{.tag} Let $K$ values of which $K - f$ honest ( $f \< K/2$ ) lying in an interval $I = [m, M]$ with honest mean $\bar g$. Then: (i) the coordinate-wise median lies in $I$, hence $\|\mathrm{med} - \bar g\| \leq M - m$; (ii) the $\beta$-trimmed mean (remove the $\beta K$ largest and smallest values, $\beta K \geq f$) is a mean of *honest* values of $I$, hence lies in $I$.

::: proof
\(i\) There are more than $K/2$ honest values: the order statistic of rank $\lceil K/2 \rceil$ is honest or bracketed by two honest values, hence in $[m, M]$; since $\bar g \in [m, M]$, the gap is at most the diameter $M - m$. (ii) With $\beta K \geq f$, the $f$ Byzantine values are numerous enough to be all removed *or* some remain — in both cases, what remains after trimming contains at least $K - 2\beta K$ values, all honest if the removed extremes cover the Byzantine ones; the mean of a subset of $[m, M]$ stays in $[m, M]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

*Scope and limits.* The guarantee is *bounded* where the mean is *arbitrary* — but it holds coordinate by coordinate: an attacker can stay "within the interval" on each coordinate while correlating its deviations to shift the global direction (dimension-by-dimension attack — the flaw exploited by El Mhamdi et al., see ch. 8); the price is also statistical: the median and trimming use information less well than the mean (efficiency $\sim 2/\pi$ in the Gaussian case for the median).
::::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 4.3 — Krum (Blanchard, El Mhamdi, Guerraoui, Stainer, NeurIPS 2017), in detail]{.tag} Parameter: an upper bound $f$ on the number of Byzantine clients, with $K \geq 2f + 3$.

1.  compute all the distances $D(i, j) = \\|g_i - g_j\\|^2$;
2.  for each $i$, score $s_i$ = sum of the $m = K - f - 2$ smallest distances $D(i, j)$ (its $m$ nearest neighbors);
3.  return $g_{i^\star}$, $i^\star = \arg\min_i s_i$ — the point most "surrounded" by close points.

::: proof
**Intuition for the guarantee.** The $K - f$ honest gradients are concentrated around the true gradient $\nabla F$ (i.i.d., variance $\sigma^2$ per coordinate): each honest point has at least $K - f - 1 \geq m + 1$ close honest neighbors, hence a score $\leq$ $(m)$ times a quantile of the inter-honest distances, of the same order as $\sigma^2 d$. A Byzantine point, on the other hand, has at most $f$ close accomplices: its score includes distances to honest points, large as soon as it moves away from the cloud — unless it *hides* inside the honest cloud, in which case it is harmless. The theorem of the paper formalizes this: under the assumption of *(2f+2, f+1)-resilience* (any mean of $f+1$ honest points is close to $\nabla F$, and $2f + 2$ honest points cannot all be simultaneously "close" to the same outlying point), the selected point is at distance $\mathcal{O}(\sigma\sqrt d)$ from the true gradient — the order of magnitude of the stochastic noise itself: robustness has not destroyed convergence. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Cost and limits.** $O(K^2 d)$ on the server (all pairwise distances); requires i.i.d. gradients — in heterogeneous federated learning (Th. 3.2), the honest points form several clusters and Krum may pick a cluster; attacks *varying over time*: alternating between two attack directions beats any one-shot selection — direct motivations for Bulyan (ch. 8).
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Geometric median and Weiszfeld iterations]{.tag} The **geometric median** $\hat g = \arg\min_x \sum_k \\|x - g_k\\|_2$ is the center minimizing the sum of distances (robust: breakdown point 1/2). Weiszfeld's algorithm (fixed point of weights inverse to the distances): $$x^{(j+1)} \;=\; \frac{\sum_k g_k \,/\, \\|x^{(j)} - g_k\\|}{\sum_k 1 \,/\, \\|x^{(j)} - g_k\\|}.$$ Each iteration is a weighted barycenter where far-away points carry little weight; convergence is guaranteed (strict convexity as soon as the $g_k$ are not aligned). **Guarantee** (RGM, Chen et al., 2017): with $f \< K/2$ and i.i.d. honest gradients of variance $\sigma^2$, $\\|\hat g - \nabla F\\| = \mathcal{O}\big(\sigma\sqrt{d/K} + \tfrac{f}{K}\big)$ up to constant factors — the price of robustness is a factor $\sqrt K$ on the stochastic part, plus a term in the fraction of corrupted clients.
:::

::: note
[The Byzantine curse of dimensionality]{.tag} The typical distance between two honest gradients grows like $\sigma\sqrt d$: in high dimension, the honest "cloud" is immense, and telling a malicious deviation from noise becomes impossible *without an additional assumption*. Impossibility results: no rule can be simultaneously unbiased (efficient at $1/\sqrt K$) and resilient to $f \> 0$ for all distributions; minimal robust estimators (trimmed mean, geometric median) incur $\Omega(\sigma\sqrt d)$ while "efficient" rules incur infinity. That is why the Byzantine setting tolerates $d = 10^3$ (aggregated gradients, cross-silo) better than $d = 10^9$ (raw LLM gradients).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Secure aggregation: pairwise masks]{.tag} Dual problem: the server must not even *see* the individual gradients (privacy, ch. 5). Bonawitz et al. (2017): each pair $(k, j)$ shares a pseudo-random seed; client $k$ sends $g_k + \sum_{j \> k} s_{kj} - \sum_{j \< k} s_{kj}$: when summing over all clients, the masks cancel out exactly ( $s_{kj} = -s_{jk}$ ) and the server only learns $\sum_k g_k$. Unexpected departures are handled by sharing the seeds via secret sharing (Shamir): the survivors reconstruct the masks of those who left. **Fundamental tension**: secure aggregation masks the individual gradients… which Krum (4.3) needs; robustness and confidentiality compete — compatible schemes (robust aggregation on cryptographically masked gradients, proofs of "proximity" to the consensus) are an active research topic (ch. 8).
:::

::: ex
[Lab experiment — attack and defense]{.tag}

```python
grads = np.array([...])                 # K honest gradients
attacker = 10 * np.linalg.norm(grads, axis=1).mean() * rng.standard_normal(d)
all_g = np.vstack([grads, attacker])   # 1 Byzantine client

mean_g   = all_g.mean(0)               # CVE: a single attacker suffices
median_g = np.median(all_g, axis=0)    # robust (Th. 4.2)

def krum(gs, f):
    D = ((gs[:, None, :] - gs[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
    K = len(gs); m = K - f - 2
    scores = np.sort(D, axis=1)[:, 1:m+1].sum(1)   # m nearest neighbors
    return gs[scores.argmin()]                     # Th. 4.3
print(np.linalg.norm(mean_g - grads.mean(0)),
      np.linalg.norm(median_g - grads.mean(0)),
      np.linalg.norm(krum(all_g, 1) - grads.mean(0)))
```

Without a defense, *a single* poisoned gradient shifts the mean by as much as desired; the median stays close to the true gradient; check that Krum indeed selects an honest gradient, then build the "dimension-by-dimension" attack (ch. 8) that traps the coordinate-wise median.
:::

## 5. Differential privacy {#ch5}

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy (Dwork)]{.tag} Two datasets $D \sim D'$ are *neighbors* if they differ in a single individual (addition/removal; some authors: replacement, i.e. Hamming distance 2 — state the convention!). A randomized algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP if for all $D \sim D'$ and every event $S$: $$\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}(D) \in S] \;\leq\; e^\varepsilon\, \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}(D') \in S] + \delta.$$ Small $\varepsilon$ ⇒ the output barely changes if one individual changes — a *computable* guarantee, composable, independent of the adversary's prior knowledge. $\delta$ allows a rare leak (typically $\delta \ll 1/n$).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Post-processing]{.tag} If $\mathcal{A}$ is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, any function $g$ applied to its output (analysis, fine-tuning, publication) is too — DP survives any *a posteriori* transformation of the results. (Proof: the likelihood ratio of $g(\mathcal{A}(D))$ inherits that of $\mathcal{A}(D)$ by change of variables — inequality of measure ratios.)
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Sequential composition (proved, case $\delta = 0$)]{.tag} If $\mathcal{A}_1$ is $\varepsilon_1$-DP and $\mathcal{A}_2$ — applied to $D$ *and to the result of $\mathcal{A}_1$* — is $\varepsilon_2$-DP, then $(\mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{A}_2)$ is $(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)$-DP: **budgets add up**.

::: proof
For any subset $S$ of the product of the outputs, conditioning on the first output $z$: $$\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{A}_2)(D) \in S] = \int \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}_1(D) = dz]\; \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}_2(D, z) \in S_z]$$ where $S_z = \{y : (z, y) \in S\}$. By DP of $\mathcal{A}_2$: $\leq e^{\varepsilon_2} \int \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}_1(D) = dz]\, \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}_2(D', z) \in S_z]$, then by DP of $\mathcal{A}_1$: $\leq e^{\varepsilon_2} e^{\varepsilon_1} \int \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}_1(D') = dz]\, \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}_2(D', z) \in S_z] = e^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}\, \mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{A}_2)(D') \in S]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

*Usage.* $T$ accesses that are $\varepsilon$-DP ⇒ $(T\varepsilon)$-DP: a naive linear budget. *Advanced* composition (Rényi DP, moments accountant, 5.5) gives $\varepsilon \sim \sqrt T$ — it is what makes DP deep learning practical.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.4 — Laplace mechanism (proved via sensitivity)]{.tag} The $\ell_1$ *sensitivity* of a query $q$ is $\Delta = \max_{D \sim D'} \\|q(D) - q(D')\\|_1$. The mechanism $M(D) = q(D) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_k)$, $Z_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon)$ i.i.d. (density $\tfrac{1}{2b}e^{-\|z\|/b}$), is $\varepsilon$-DP.

::: proof
For any output $z$, the ratio of densities satisfies, by the triangle inequality: $$\frac{p_M(z \mid D)}{p_M(z \mid D')} = \exp\Big(-\tfrac{\\|z - q(D)\\|_1 - \\|z - q(D')\\|_1}{b}\Big) \;\leq\; \exp\Big(\tfrac{\\|q(D) - q(D')\\|_1}{b}\Big) \;\leq\; e^{\Delta/b} = e^{\varepsilon},$$ with $b = \Delta/\varepsilon$. Since the density ratio is uniformly bounded by $e^\varepsilon$, so is the ratio of the probabilities of any event: $\varepsilon$-DP. [∎]{.qed}
:::

*Added error.* $\mathbb{E}\|Z\| = b = \Delta/\varepsilon$ (per coordinate): the noise is proportional to the sensitivity — hence the art of DP: rewriting queries to minimize $\Delta$. **Gaussian**: for $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$, $\sigma \geq \Delta_2 \sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon$ gives $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP (proof via a Gaussian tail bound; $\ell_2$ noise is the right regime for training).
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.5 — DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016) and the moments accountant]{.tag}

1.  clip each gradient *per example*: $\tilde g_i = g_i / \max(1, \\|g_i\\|_2/C)$ — bounds the sensitivity: changing one individual changes the sum of the clipped gradients by at most $\sim 2C$;
2.  add noise to the batch: $\tilde g = \frac1m\big(\sum_i \tilde g_i + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 C^2 I)\big)$;
3.  take the SGD step with $\tilde g$.

**Moments accountant (statement).** For a mechanism $M$, define the Rényi moment of order $\lambda$: $M_M(\lambda) = \max_{D \sim D'} \log \mathbb{E}_{z \sim M(D')} \big[\big(\tfrac{p_M(z\|D)}{p_M(z\|D')}\big)^\lambda\big]$: composition *adds the moments* ($T$ steps: total moment $T \cdot M_M(\lambda)$), and conversion to DP gives $$\varepsilon \;=\; \min_\lambda \frac{T\, M_M(\lambda) - \log \delta}{\lambda},$$ that is, typically $\varepsilon = \Theta(\sqrt T)$ instead of $T$ — a quadratic gain on the budget. It is this accountant (implemented in the Opacus/TensorFlow Privacy libraries) that tracks the budget at every step of training. *Fundamental trade-off*: utility $\leftrightarrow$ privacy $\leftrightarrow$ amount of data (the noise, fixed at $C$, gets averaged over large batches: DP likes large $n$).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — Local vs central DP]{.tag} **Central**: a trusted curator adds the noise (the mechanisms above): good utility/privacy ratio. **Local**: each user randomizes *before* sending (no trust required — the keyboard model): the variance accumulates per user, and utility drops (randomized response for counts); the *shuffle* model (anonymization by cryptographic mixing) sits between the two. Rule of thumb: local for extremely sensitive data, central for research, shuffle for real systems.
:::

::: ex
[Membership inference attack — how it works]{.tag} The adversary's goal: decide whether the example $x$ was in the training set. Protocol (Shokri et al., 2017): (i) train *shadow models* on similar data whose member/non-member status is known; (ii) learn a small classifier separating the confidence scores of members vs non-members; (iii) apply it to the confidences of the target model. The exploited signal: *memorization* — the model is more confident on its training data; the worst memorization concerns "atypical" data (canaries: Carlini et al., 2019, demonstrate verbatim extraction of inserted secrets). DP bounds this signal: the influence of an example on any output is capped by clipping + noise; conversely, an attack rate close to chance is an empirical privacy *test*.
:::

::: note
[Why LLGA cares]{.tag} LLMs memorize training fragments (extraction attacks); DP training (DP-SGD on fine-tuning) is an active defense — and the M2 module "Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs" extends exactly this chapter. In the federated setting, DP and secure aggregation (4.5) combine: cryptographic masks against the server, DP against *a posteriori* adversaries. Graph confidentiality (node-DP, edge-DP) protects social networks — see the Graph ML module. Multi-agent systems (see the Reinforcement Learning module, ch. 7) raise the same question: what do interaction logs leak?
:::

## 6. Collaboration, personalization, fairness {#ch6}

-   **Personalization**: a global model + local heads (light per-client fine-tuning); Bayesian interpretation (mixture of posteriors); multi-task formalization (Ditto, ch. 3);
-   **Model fusion and mode connectivity**: two networks trained from the *same* initialization are connected by a nearly flat path in the loss surface (low barrier along the segment — Frankle et al., 2020); consequence for collaboration: local models can be *averaged*… provided they stay in the same basin; realigning the neuron permutations between two models is the key to recent fusions (sketch); these are the theoretical foundations of FedAvg (the averaging of chapter 3 only makes sense in this regime);
-   **Data markets**: valuing a data source by its marginal contribution — Shapley value $\phi_i = \sum_{S \ni i}$ \[gain of the model with $S$ minus without $i$\] (estimated by Monte-Carlo permutations); data buyers/sellers, incentives for quality — game theory meets ML;
-   **Vertical FL**: clients hold different *features* about the same individuals (bank × retailer): split learning, exchanges of protected intermediate representations — a complement to the "horizontal" FL of ch. 3;
-   **Fairness**: performance per subgroup (demographic parity, equalized odds); in the federated setting, fairness cuts across clients; the *Computational Optimal Transport* module provides tools (barycenters, fairness via OT);
-   **Toward multi-agent systems**: when "workers" become *LLM agents*, collaboration becomes orchestration (roles, votes, verification) — the loop is closed with the Reinforcement Learning and Autonomous Agents module, chapter 7; the mechanisms of this module (robust aggregation, budgets, incentives) carry over directly.

## 7. Scaling and compute {#ch7}

::: thm
[Theorem 7.1 — Scaling laws (Kaplan 2020, Chinchilla 2022): formulas and reading]{.tag} On large corpora, the validation loss follows a power law in parameters $N$ and tokens $D$ (before the saturation regime): $$\text{Kaplan: } L(N, D) = \Big[\Big(\frac{N_c}{N}\Big)^{\alpha_N/\alpha_D} + \frac{D_c}{D}\Big]^{\alpha_D}, \qquad \text{Chinchilla: } L = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}},$$ with for Chinchilla $\alpha \approx 0.34$, $\beta \approx 0.28$, and $E \approx 1.69$ the irreducible loss (entropy of language); $A, B, N_c, D_c$ are calibrated constants. Training compute is billed $C \approx 6\,N D$ FLOPs (2 passes × 3 per parameter/token).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — Compute-optimal: the Chinchilla derivation]{.tag} Minimize $L = E + A N^{-\alpha} + B D^{-\beta}$ under the budget $6 N D = C$: the Lagrange conditions ($-\alpha A N^{-\alpha - 1} = 6\lambda D$ and $-\beta B D^{-\beta - 1} = 6\lambda N$) give $$\alpha A\, N^{-\alpha} = \beta B\, D^{-\beta} \;\Rightarrow\; N^\star \propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)} \approx C^{0.45}, \qquad D^\star \propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)} \approx C^{0.55},$$ that is: **N and D grow together, almost like $\sqrt C$**, with a ratio $D^\star/N^\star \approx 20$ tokens per parameter (empirical value: \~1.4T tokens for 70B parameters). Counter-intuitive but verified: Chinchilla (70B) beats Gopher (280B) trained on the same compute; the models of the Kaplan generation were *undertrained* (too many parameters, too few tokens per parameter). LLGA reading: compute is the scarce resource; power laws justify budgets; "emergent capabilities" are the deviations (thresholds) beyond this smooth law — see the M2 Large Language Models module.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — Mixture of Experts: decoupling FLOPs from parameters]{.tag} An MoE replaces each feed-forward layer with $E$ "experts" and a router that activates only the top $k$ (top-1 in Switch Transformer, Fedus et al., 2021) per token: the *parameters* grow with $E$ (up to a trillion), while the *FLOPs per token* stay nearly constant — the Chinchilla law recalibrates on this distinction between active and latent parameters. Technical points: capacity factor (load per expert), balancing loss (preventing routing collapse), all-to-all communication (link to ch. 2).
:::

::: note
[Federating LLM training: where do we stand?]{.tag} The previous chapters combine into a "federated LLM": cross-silo (ch. 3) LoRA adapters (FedIT, ch. 3), compression of exchanges (QSGD/error feedback, ch. 2), robust aggregation (ch. 4) if some silos are hostile, DP (ch. 5) for sensitive prompts, and compute-optimality (7.2) to decide *where* to place the parameters. None of these ingredients alone makes the recipe: that is exactly the state of the art — and an M2 project topic (ML Ops / LLMs).
:::

## 8. Course research notes — CMAP (El Mhamdi, Dieuleveut) {#ch8}

The official team of the 2026-2027 course unit (SynapseS sheet) is El Mahdi El Mhamdi & Paul Mangold (CMAP, École Polytechnique). This chapter presents the work of El Mhamdi (section 8.1, the foundation of the robustness strand of the course) and that of Aymeric Dieuleveut (section 8.2, CMAP): foundational works of the stochastic optimization and federated strand that the team in place extends — excellent leads for the **research project** which serves as the official assessment of the course unit.

### 8.1. El Mahdi El Mhamdi — Byzantine tolerance for distributed ML

The guiding thread: *can we learn in a distributed way when some participants lie?* — a line of research that founded the field (byzantine-ML) whose chapters 2-4 this course follows.

::: thm
[Work 8.1 — Krum (Blanchard, El Mhamdi, Guerraoui, Stainer, NeurIPS 2017)]{.tag} First aggregation rule *provably* tolerant to Byzantine clients for distributed SGD (Algorithm 4.3): selection of the most surrounded point, guarantee of distance $\mathcal{O}(\sigma\sqrt d)$ to the true gradient under iid, cost $O(K^2 d)$. Published at the moment distributed SGD was becoming the industrial standard — \~4000 citations; it is the reference that all subsequent GARs (geometric median, trimmed, Bulyan) discuss.
:::

::: thm
[Work 8.2 — The Hidden Vulnerability & Bulyan (El Mhamdi, Guerraoui, Rouault, ICML 2018)]{.tag} **Negative result.** *Coordinate-wise* rules (median, trimmed mean — Th. 4.2) are beaten by a "dimension-by-dimension" attack: the attacker stays within the honest interval on each coordinate while correlating its deviations — the global direction drifts; and any rule that *selects a point* (Krum!) can be forced to pick a bad point under attacks varying over time. **Constructive answer:** *Bulyan* — iterate Krum to select $K - f - 4$ candidates, then *coordinate-wise* trimmed means *on the selected candidates*: the selection filters out outliers, the trimming neutralizes the remaining corrupted ones; convergence is proven at the price of a residual bias and an increased variance (the $1/\sqrt K$ becomes $1/\sqrt{K - 4f}$ up to a constant). Methodological lesson: *impossibility first* — characterize what no GAR can do, then build under these bounds.
:::

::: note
[What next?]{.tag} The program continues: *Distributed Momentum for Byzantine-resilient SGD* (ICLR 2021) — making the *momentum* variant robust (the optimizer's memory accumulation enlarges the attack surface, see Proposition 0.4); and more broadly the safety of distributed learning systems: interactions between robustness (ch. 4), confidentiality (secure aggregation, ch. 5) and verifiability — the "complete security" of a federated system is a multi-objective problem, not an accumulation of patches.
:::

### 8.2. Aymeric Dieuleveut — stochastic acceleration and the federated setting

::: thm
[Work 8.3 — Optimal averaged SGD (Dieuleveut, Flammarion, Bach, JMLR 2017)]{.tag} *Statement (finite-dimensional case).* For least-squares regression (quadratic function, noise $\sigma^2$, dimension $d$, condition number $\kappa$), SGD *with Polyak-Ruppert averaging* — and its "tail averaging" version $\bar\theta_n = \tfrac{2}{n}\sum_{t \> n/2} \theta_t$ which discards the first iterations — with step size $\eta \propto 1/\sqrt n$ reaches $$\mathbb{E}\big[F(\bar\theta_n)\big] - F^\star \;\leq\; \mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{d\,\sigma^2}{n}\Big) \qquad \text{(minimax rate, without knowing } \sigma^2 \text{ or the spectrum)},$$ where plain SGD with a constant step size plateaus at $\sigma/\sqrt n$ (Theorem 0.1) and would require exact knowledge of the constants to be optimal. *Idea.* Averaging decouples bias and variance: the individual iterates remain noisy, but their average estimates the optimum asymptotically *without bias* (the noise averages out at rate $1/n$, the deterministic dynamics converge fast). It is the tool that makes SGD "parameter-free" — behind the practical optimizers of the module and the optimal Nadaraya-Watson-type rates in the nonparametric setting.
:::

::: thm
[Work 8.4 — Federated-EM (Dieuleveut, Fort, Moulines, Robin, NeurIPS 2021)]{.tag} First federated extension of the EM algorithm to models with latent variables (Gaussian mixtures, HMMs): each client computes its local E statistics, the server aggregates and performs the M step. *Result.* A version with **control variates** (the SCAFFOLD/SVRG motif — Propositions 0.3 and 3.5!) corrects heterogeneity and variance: convergence is proven toward a neighborhood of the optimum at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/R)$ in rounds, with radius controlled by heterogeneity and mitigated by the correction — the same theorem as 3.3, transposed to EM steps. Applications: federated GMMs in healthcare, federated HMMs in telephony; extended by Federated Majorize-Minimization (2025), which unifies these constructions beyond the server parameter.
:::

::: note
[And also: communication]{.tag} Artemis (Philippenko & Dieuleveut, 2020): *tight* bounds for bidirectional compression (server ⇄ clients, ch. 2) in heterogeneous federated learning — when the download AND the upload are compressed, memory is needed (error feedback on both sides) to preserve the rate. The guiding thread of this work: *making the guarantees of chapter 0 robust to the realities of chapters 2-3* (expensive communication, heterogeneity, statistical variance of clients).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **Batch variance.** Show that the variance of the batch gradient of size $m$ is $\sigma^2/m$, and deduce the "linear speedup" of distributed SGD (with $K$ workers, same steps, same iterations: error $\sigma/\sqrt{Km}$).
2.  **SGD recursion.** Detail the three ingredients of step 2 of Theorem 0.1 (convexity, bias-variance decomposition, smoothness inequality) and verify the telescoping step; what happens if $\eta \> 1/L$?
3.  **FedAvg = SGD when $E = 1$.** Verify that FedAvg with a single local epoch recovers exactly distributed SGD, then simulate client drift on heterogeneous quadratic data ($F_k$ with different minimizers) for $E \in \{1, 5, 20\}$ and recover the bias of Theorem 3.2 (with $a_1 = 1, a_2 = 10$).
4.  **Exact SCAFFOLD on the quadratic.** On the example of Theorem 3.2, show that with the exact control variates $c_k - c = a_k(\theta - z_k) - \bar a(\theta - \bar z)$, the corrected local update uses the *global* gradient — and hence that the fixed point becomes $\theta^\star$ again.
5.  **Robust median.** Show that if $f \< K/2$ gradients are arbitrary, the coordinate-wise median stays at bounded distance from the median of the honest gradients, unlike the mean (give an explicit attack on the mean).
6.  **Krum in practice.** Implement Krum (code of ch. 4), then the "dimension-by-dimension" attack: show that an attacker who sends the honest mean gradient plus an alternating $\pm\delta$ per coordinate traps the coordinate-wise median but not (immediately) Krum; discuss.
7.  **Geometric median.** Implement Weiszfeld (Proposition 4.4) on Gaussian gradients + one outlying attacker; compare convergence radius and robustness with the coordinate-wise median.
8.  **DP of the counting query.** For the query "how many individuals have property $P$?", show that the release $q(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)$ is $\varepsilon$-DP (sensitivity 1), and compute the typical error.
9.  **Composition.** Prove Theorem 5.3 in the case of three nested mechanisms, then compute the total budget of 100 queries that are $\varepsilon_0$-DP under simple composition; comment on the gap with advanced composition ($\sim\sqrt T$).
10. **Gossip.** Simulate gossip aggregation $\theta^{(k)} \leftarrow \theta^{(k)} + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(k)}(\theta^{(j)} - \theta^{(k)})$ on a cycle then on a complete graph; relate the speed to the second eigenvalue of the Laplacian (spectrum = Graph ML module).
11. **Chinchilla on paper.** Redo the derivation of Theorem 7.2 with $\alpha = 0.34$, $\beta = 0.28$: compute the exponents of $N^\star$ and $D^\star$ in $C$; for $C = 10^{23}$ FLOPs, deduce an order of magnitude of $N^\star$ (with the constants of the paper: $A \approx 406$, $B \approx 410$) and the tokens/parameters ratio.

::: note
[Solutions — exercises 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9, 11]{.tag}

**1.** Independence: $\mathrm{Var}(\tfrac1m\sum_i g_i) = \tfrac{1}{m^2} m\sigma^2 = \sigma^2/m$. For $K$ workers with i.i.d. batches of size $m$, the aggregate has variance $\sigma^2/(Km)$ — plug into Theorem 0.1 (replace $\sigma$ by $\sigma/\sqrt{Km}$): for a fixed total number of examples consumed, the same error as sequentially — but each step cost a $1/K$-th of the time (parallel computation): this is the speedup, valid if communication is free (Theorem 2.2 for the full version).

**2.** (i) convexity: $f(\theta^\star) \geq f(\theta_t) + \langle\nabla f(\theta_t), \theta^\star - \theta_t\rangle$; (ii) $\mathbb{E}\\|g\\|^2 = \\|\nabla f\\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\\|\xi\\|^2$, then $\tfrac12\\|\nabla f(\theta)\\|^2 \leq L(f(\theta) - f^\star)$ (smoothness + convexity); (iii) telescoping: $\sum_t (\mathbb{E}D_t - \mathbb{E}D_{t+1}) = D_0 - \mathbb{E}D_T \leq D^2$. If $\eta \> 2/L$: $1 - \eta L \< 0$, the recursion no longer controls anything — the optimal deterministic step $\eta = 1/L$ stays below the $2/L$ bar set by the noise.

**3.** $E = 1$: $\theta_{r+1} = \frac1K\sum_k(\theta_r - \eta g_k(\theta_r)) = \theta_r - \eta \bar g(\theta_r)$ — exact distributed SGD. For the drift: apply Theorem 3.2 (values: fixed point $\approx 0.713$ versus optimum $\approx 0.909$); at $E = 1$ the bias vanishes ($c_1 = c_2 = 1 - \eta$, mean and optimum coincide), it grows with $E$ — plot $\|\theta_\infty - \theta^\star\|$ as a function of $E$.

**5.** The mean: an attacker sends $C = \frac{K-f}{f}\,\bar g_{\mathrm{hon}} + \delta$ and shifts the mean by $\delta/f$ in the desired direction — arbitrary. The median: with $K - f \> K/2$ honest values in $[m, M]$, the median lies in $[m, M]$ (Theorem 4.2); the gap to the honest median is at most the diameter of the honest part — *bounded* independently of the attack.

**8.** Sensitivity: adding/removing one individual changes $q$ by at most 1, so $\Delta = 1$; Theorem 5.4 gives $\varepsilon$-DP for $b = 1/\varepsilon$. Typical error: $\mathbb{E}\|Z\| = 1/\varepsilon$ (one "blurred" individual at $\varepsilon = 1$; at $\varepsilon = 0.1$, ten — hence the price of strong DP on small counts).

**9.** Three mechanisms: apply the nesting of Theorem 5.3 twice ($\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \varepsilon_3$). One hundred $\varepsilon_0$-DP queries: $100\,\varepsilon_0$ under simple composition; advanced composition (moments accountant, 5.5) gives roughly $\varepsilon \approx \sqrt{2 \times 100 \ln(1.25/\delta)}\,\varepsilon_0$ (at $\delta = 10^{-6}$: $\approx 63\,\varepsilon_0$) — better, but still growing: DP taxes every access, definitively.

**11.** Exponents: $\beta/(\alpha+\beta) = 0.28/0.62 \approx 0.45$ for $N^\star$, $0.34/0.62 \approx 0.55$ for $D^\star$. With $C = 10^{23}$: the Lagrange condition gives $N \approx 1.7\, D^{0.82}$, and $6ND = C$ solves to $D^\star \approx 1.1 \times 10^{12}$ tokens and $N^\star \approx 1.5 \times 10^{10}$ parameters (order of magnitude, parametric fit); the ratio $D^\star/N^\star$ comes out between 20 and 80 depending on the fitting method of the paper (IsoFLOP vs parametric) — two figures, one single lesson: at a fixed budget, *feed the model with tokens* rather than inflating the parameters.
:::
